chapter: New York, church bands and early training
title: Why reading mattered and how white musicians took over the work
summary: He says Black New York musicians had to read stock arrangements, and that white players with conservatory training came in and borrowed ideas they heard.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: They had everything, so who provided most of their work, I don't know. It probably was an evolution, 'cause contrary
Briggs
to what most people think, the black musicians were not musicians at all. In my time, if you couldn't read you didn't have a chance.
Right.

To play dance schools and things, you had to read. You had what you call the stock arrangements, you get it from the editors, and you had to read it. If you couldn't read, you didn't have a chance. I believe that the majority of the guys who have bad impressions were those who had not had any instrumental training, instrumental or musical training.
Right.
That is the tonic solfege, everything.
Right.
You see, that's what I'm saying.
Right.
But in my time, as I
Briggs
said in my reference to the Lincoln Theater, you ever heard of it --
Oh yes, sure.

Well, you see, that's how it happened. And we had two or three movie picture houses that had small orchestras and the same thing happened there. Phone so and so and says, "He's sick today, could you send me a trumpet or a violin or a viola or something violin cello or something." So, you see that if you couldn't read it's another thing.
So you're expected to just go right out there and sight-read the job?
Yes. That's it, yes. And I'm very thankful to Mr. Eugene Mikell for giving me a very good theoretical musical education. I continued naturally.
You started right off as a reader?
Right.
Briggs
So it wasn't like those early jazz players in New Orleans, a lot of them couldn't read.
That's right, couldn't read, no.
But you were a trained musician.
Yes, yes, that's the difference, you see.
Right.
Yes.
Well, tell me about that, what happened then that the white guys began to move in and take over a lot of that work.
Well, I'll tell you what happened. The white boys had theoretical training. The majority of them studied harmony.
Right.
And everything else. They were permitted to go to conservatories.
Briggs
And they studied and everything, and this is the truth, they would come around and listen to certain formations, colored formations playing, and jot down certain things that they hear.
Right. I see.
And use the same, and develop their own ideas with it.
I see.
